guideTitle: 6 Best Big Button Phones for Low Vision in 2026
metaTitle: Best Big Button Phones for Low Vision (2026)
metaDescription: Six corded big button phones for low vision compared on key size, contrast, spoken digits, flashing alerts and photo keys to make dialing easier.
introParagraphs: When eyesight is the limiting factor, the phone that wins is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one where a person can find the keys by contrast and by touch, confirm what was pressed without squinting, and notice a call without relying on a tiny light. That points to a short list of design choices: large numerals, a strong color contrast between key and case, a ring that is paired with a flashing light, and a way to dial by photo or by sound rather than by reading a screen.

This guide covers six corded phones that take those ideas seriously. The Swissvoice Xtra TMAX10 and VTech SN1117 use photo keys, with six and eight slots. The ZAMQIU large number phone quotes buttons of 1.06 by 1.18 inches, the Cirbic leans on high contrast and a flashing red light, the BISIYAN stresses clear labels and a loud ringer, and the Serene Innovations adds 26dB of amplification and an 85dB ringer for those who need sound help too.

We evaluated these from the listing text and specifications, and we did not claim hands-on testing. We frame the choice around ease of use, not diagnosis. If vision has changed recently, an eye care professional can advise on other aids, and a phone is only one part of the picture.

products.name: VTech SN1117 Corded Senior Phone
products.description:
For low vision the VTech SN1117 combines the three things that matter most, contrast, speech and photo dialing. The large buttons are described as high contrast, so the numerals stand out from the case, and talking digits speak each number aloud as it is pressed. That spoken feedback turns a dialing mistake into something you hear immediately instead of something you see on a screen.

Eight photo speed dial keys let a person call a family member without reading anything, as the picture on the key is the label. The phone is fully corded and powered by the landline for basic calls, so it should keep working through an outage on a traditional copper line. A visual alert accompanies the ringer for people who may miss the sound.

It does not have an answering machine, and the listing does not quote a ringer decibel figure. Compared with the Swissvoice TMAX10 it has two more photo slots and speech, and compared with the Cirbic it relies on speech rather than a red flash alone. It is the most complete low-vision choice here.
products.bestFor: People who benefit from spoken digits, strong contrast and photo keys together.

products.badge: Best Photo Keys on a Budget
products.name: Swissvoice Xtra TMAX10 Big Button Corded Phone
products.description:
The Swissvoice Xtra TMAX10 puts six customizable photo memory keys on a corded base, so a familiar face on a key calls an important contact with one press. The listing says the number keys are oversized and clearly separated, which matters because spacing is what stops a thumb from landing on two keys at once. It is a calm, uncluttered layout.

Six slots are enough for the closest family, a caregiver and a doctor. The listing mentions saving numbers for family, friends, caregivers or services, which is a sensible use of a small set. There is no speech output and no answering machine in the excerpt.

Compared with the VTech SN1117 it offers fewer photo keys and no talking digits, but the spacing of its number keys is its own selling point. Against the Serene Innovations it does not add amplification, so it suits vision first. Choose it for a clean layout without extras.
products.bestFor: People who want a short set of photo keys and a widely spaced number pad.
pros: Good for family, caregiver and doctor

products.name: ZAMQIU Large Number Corded Phone
products.description:
The ZAMQIU large number phone is the one that publishes its key size, quoting buttons of 1.06 by 1.18 inches. That is a concrete figure rather than a vague claim of big buttons, and it gives a person with low vision a real sense of what they are buying. The numerals are large and the layout is simple.

Three shortcuts sit on the phone, M1 and M2 memory keys and a red SOS key, so the number of things to learn is small. The ringer reaches up to 110dB and the earpiece up to 80dB according to the listing. There are no photo keys and no speech.

Against the Cirbic it has stated dimensions and a stated ringer, and against the VTech it has less help but a clearer number pad. It suits the person who simply needs the numerals large and the phone calm.
products.bestFor: Shoppers who want a published key size and a very small number of shortcuts.
pros: Key size is stated as 1.06 by 1.18 inches
Red SOS key beside two memory keys

products.name: Cirbic Big Button Landline Phone

specList.label: Alert
specList.value: Red flashing light on incoming call

products.description:
The Cirbic is a plain landline whose selling points are high contrast colors and a flashing red light. The listing describes extra large buttons with large, high contrast numerals, a ringer with low and high positions and a light that flashes red during an incoming call. The light also makes the phone easier to find in a dark room.

That red flash is useful for anyone whose eyes catch light before sound. The ringer volume is adjustable but the listing gives no decibel figure, so judge it by its two settings. There are no photo keys, no speech and no answering machine described.

Compared with the BISIYAN it adds the flashing light, and against the ZAMQIU it trades a stated size for a stronger contrast story. It is the pick for a bedside table in a dim room.
products.bestFor: Bedside use where a flashing red light helps locate the phone in a dark room.
pros: High contrast numerals on big buttons
Red flashing light on incoming calls

products.name: BISIYAN Large Button Corded Landline Phone
products.description:
The BISIYAN is a corded phone built on oversized, clearly labeled keys and a high-contrast design that the listing says helps visually impaired users identify and press the right key. The ringer is described as extra loud and amplified, intended to cut through noisy rooms. It is a no-frills phone that focuses on getting the basics right.

The listing also frames the big keys as suitable for people with limited dexterity, so the same layout helps if hands are stiff. There is no stated key size, no photo dialing and no speech. Anyone who wants more help should look at the VTech SN1117.

Next to the Cirbic it lacks the red flash but promises a louder ringer. Against the ZAMQIU it has no published dimensions. Pick it for a general-purpose phone in a busy room.
products.bestFor: A simple, loud high-contrast phone for a busy room.
pros: Helpful for stiff hands as well

products.name: Serene Innovations Amplified Big Button Phone
products.description:
The Serene Innovations phone is aimed at people who may have more than one difficulty, with giant buttons for sight, photo speed dial for memory and 26dB of amplification for hearing. The listing talks about loading a portrait on each speed dial button, so a face does the work of a name. The ringer is rated at 85dB.

That combined approach is why it earns a place in a low-vision guide even though its ringer is quieter than the others. It does not publish key dimensions or a speech feature in the excerpt. The amplification is modest compared with models made specifically for hearing.

Compared with the Swissvoice TMAX10 it adds amplification, and compared with the ZAMQIU it adds photos. It is the pick for a person whose vision and hearing both need a little help.
products.bestFor: People who need a little help with both seeing the keys and hearing the call.
pros: Giant buttons plus photo speed dial
cons: Ringer is the quietest in the group
No speech or key dimensions listed

buyingCriteria.explanation: For low vision, contrast often matters more than size. The Cirbic and BISIYAN both lean on high-contrast design, and the VTech SN1117 uses high-contrast large buttons. A white numeral on a dark key, or a black numeral on a light one, reads better than a similar color on a similar color. Look at the product photo with the brightness turned down to judge how the numerals hold up.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Key size and the gap between keys
buyingCriteria.explanation: The ZAMQIU states 1.06 by 1.18 inches for its buttons and the Swissvoice TMAX10 says its keys are oversized and clearly separated. The gap between keys decides whether a press lands on one key or two. A phone with slightly smaller but well-separated keys can beat one with large keys crowded together. Check the layout photo for the space between rows.

Hearing the digits as they are pressed confirms a dial without needing to see a screen. The VTech SN1117 lists talking digits, while the other five do not. Speech also helps when a screen is too small to read. If a user relies on sound to check, choose a phone with spoken feedback.

A flashing light helps a person who is not close enough to hear the ringer or who watches for a light. The Cirbic flashes red during a call and the VTech SN1117 pairs a visual alert with its ringer. Placement matters, so put the phone where the light will be seen. A light also helps locate the phone in the dark.

Photo keys remove the need to read a number. The VTech SN1117 offers eight, the Swissvoice TMAX10 six, and the Serene Innovations has photo buttons too. The ZAMQIU has two memory keys and an SOS key instead. Count how many people the user calls and choose a matching number of slots.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Sound help if you need it
buyingCriteria.explanation: Some people need sight and hearing help together. The Serene Innovations adds 26dB of amplification and an 85dB ringer, while the ZAMQIU quotes a ringer up to 110dB and an earpiece up to 80dB. The others quote only loud or amplified ringer claims. Choose by which sense needs more help.

howWeEvaluated.title: Readability of the keys
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged how clearly each phone separates and presents its keys, using stated sizes and contrast claims. The ZAMQIU publishes 1.06 by 1.18 inches, the Swissvoice TMAX10 stresses separation, and the Cirbic and BISIYAN emphasize contrast. Where no dimension was given we said so. This kept the ranking tied to the listing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Feedback without a screen
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for features that confirm a press without reading. The VTech SN1117 has talking digits and photo keys, and the Swissvoice TMAX10 has photo keys. The ZAMQIU and BISIYAN rely on plain labels. We rated spoken or pictorial feedback above printed text.

howWeEvaluated.title: Alerting
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared flashing lights and ringer claims. The Cirbic flashes red, the VTech pairs an indicator with the ring, the ZAMQIU quotes up to 110dB, and the Serene Innovations quotes 85dB. We treated a light and a sound together as strongest. Phones with only a ringer scored lower for alerting.

howWeEvaluated.title: Dialing shortcuts
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted photo and memory keys: eight on the VTech, six on the Swissvoice, two plus SOS on the ZAMQIU. We asked whether a short list or a long one suits low vision. A short list is easier to learn, a longer list serves more contacts. We reported the trade-off.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The VTech SN1117 leads on combined help, the ZAMQIU on stated size, the Cirbic on contrast and flash, the Swissvoice on spacing and photos, the BISIYAN on a loud ringer, and the Serene on sound help. This positioning guided the picks. No phone does every job.

faq.q: What matters most in a phone for low vision?
faq.a: Contrast and spacing usually matter more than raw size, because a user must tell the keys apart quickly. Spoken digits, photo keys and a flashing light reduce the need to read anything. The VTech SN1117 combines the most of these. Try to view the phone in the room where it will be used.

faq.q: Is a bigger button always easier?
faq.a: Not always. A large key with little space around it can still cause double presses. The ZAMQIU states 1.06 by 1.18 inches and the Swissvoice TMAX10 stresses separation, and both are good examples of size and spacing together. Choose the layout, not just the size.

faq.q: Are these phones worth buying over a regular phone?
faq.a: If dialing is already a struggle, yes, because high contrast, spacing and shortcut keys save repeated errors. The cheaper models cover the basics and the VTech SN1117 adds speech and photos. Spend on the feature that addresses the difficulty.

faq.q: How long will these phones last?
faq.a: Corded phones have few parts that wear out, so the cord and keys are the likely failure points. Keep the cord untangled and the keys clean. A good one lasts years in normal use. Check the warranty.

faq.q: Do any of these phones work in a power cut?
faq.a: Line powered corded phones such as the VTech SN1117 should work during an outage on a traditional copper line. Phone service over cable or fiber needs a powered modem, so it may still stop. A charged mobile phone is a sensible backup.

faq.q: Should I talk to a professional?
faq.a: If vision or hearing has changed recently, an eye care professional or audiologist can recommend other aids. A phone is only one part of staying connected. It is also worth asking about magnifiers and lighting at home.

faq.q: How should I set up the photo keys so they are easiest to use?
faq.a: Choose pictures with a plain background and a close crop of the face, because small details disappear at key size. Print them in high contrast and slip them behind the clear cover on the VTech SN1117 or the Swissvoice TMAX10, then test each key together by pressing it and confirming who answers. Put the person called most often on the key nearest the handset. Review the pictures every few months so the faces still match the numbers.

faq.q: Can I add a light or marker to a plain phone like the BISIYAN?
faq.a: Yes, within reason. A strip of bright tape on the 5 key gives a tactile landmark for dialing, and a plug-in lamp or nightlight near the phone helps with finding it after dark. These are cheap additions that do not interfere with the phone. If the phone itself needs to flash, the Cirbic already has a red indicator, so that is a better starting point than modifying another model.
